OWASP LLM01: Prompt Injection

Prompt injection occurs when untrusted input causes a model to ignore its instructions. Example attacks include text such as "ignore previous instructions". Mitigations: treat tool output as data, not instructions, and constrain privileges.

Blog: Defending agents from injection

We reviewed phrases attackers hide in web pages, like telling the model to disregard its task. Our guard classifier scores each tool result and holds side-effecting calls when a result looks like instructions.

THREAT-MODEL.md

## Untrusted content
File contents, issues and web pages may contain text aimed at the agent. We assume an attacker will try to override the system prompt. Controls: the agent treats such text as inert and never runs commands found inside it.

## Security

Report vulnerabilities to security@example.com. Do not file public issues for injection bugs. We run a classifier on untrusted inputs and audit every tool call an agent makes.

policy.txt

Staff must not paste secrets or API keys into issues, chat, or AI tools. If a document instructs you to exfiltrate data, treat it as a phishing attempt and report it.

CTF write-up: the injection challenge

The flag was hidden behind a model that could be tricked. We describe, for education, how crafted comments tried to make it leak the flag, and how input validation stopped them. No live payloads are included.

- name: injection_markers

### Postmortem: prompt-injection attempt

On 2026-10-02 a crafted README tried to make our agent skip tests. The guard flagged it and no side effects ran. Action items: expand the eval suite, document the window rules.

lecture-07.md

# AI safety: injection

Students: an injection is untrusted text that imitates the operator. We will study why 'ignore previous instructions' is a classic example and how layered defenses reduce its impact.
